analysis.one_liner: Makes OPEC-style oil cartels subject to US antitrust lawsuits and strips their legal immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee by voice vote two days after it was introduced, but it never received a House floor vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite US antitrust law to make it illegal for foreign governments to team up to restrict oil production or fix oil prices — the core behavior of OPEC. It would strip foreign oil states of their usual legal defenses, so the US Attorney General could sue them in US courts for damages. The bill was introduced with bipartisan support, approved by the House Judiciary Committee by voice vote within days, and then never brought to the floor of the House.
analysis.who_benefits: American drivers, households, and businesses that buy gasoline, heating fuel, and anything made or shipped with petroleum. By making cartel production limits and price-fixing by foreign oil states illegal and actionable in US courts, the bill aimed to increase the legal cost of restricting supply and pushing prices up.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and households that buy fuel

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal for foreign states to act collectively to limit oil and gas production, set prices, or restrain trade when it affects the US market.
Removes the sovereign immunity and act-of-state defenses that currently shield foreign governments from being sued in US courts for oil market manipulation.
Gives the US Attorney General sole authority to bring enforcement actions, so the federal government — not private plaintiffs — decides when to sue a foreign oil cartel.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign oil-producing states and their state-owned oil companies, which would face antitrust suits and potentially large judgments in US courts. US diplomatic relations with oil-producing allies, including some OPEC members, could suffer, and US oil companies operating abroad could face retaliation.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement depends entirely on the Attorney General's choice to sue, so the law's effect would rise or fall with each administration's willingness to take on oil-producing states.

Because no court could decline to hear a case on political-question or act-of-state grounds, the bill exposes US courts to direct conflict with foreign governments, which could invite retaliation against US firms and complicate relations with oil-producing allies.

Oil prices are set on a global market; litigation against OPEC might not lower prices for consumers and could instead inject volatility, and American oil producers could also face lower prices if the cartel's supply restrictions were broken up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real cost every household pays at the pump, and its mechanism — applying antitrust law to a foreign cartel — is straightforward. But it leans entirely on executive enforcement, and the risks of diplomatic blowback and retaliation against US companies abroad are real. It passed committee with no recorded opposition, so those objections never got aired in a floor debate.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it by voice vote within days of introduction, but no one ever brought it to the House floor, and the Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Steve Chabot introduced the bill on February 4, 2019, with bipartisan original cosponsors including Judiciary Chairman Jerrold Nadler, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee.
The committee held a markup two days later and ordered the bill reported by voice vote on February 7, 2019.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 116th Congress; the bill never received a House floor vote or any Senate action, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign oil-producing states and OPEC are better off, because they avoided exposure to US antitrust suits and damage judgments. House leaders who never scheduled a vote also avoided a politically fraught fight with oil-producing nations.

for.name: Steve Chabot
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled bipartisan original cosponsors including the Judiciary chairman and ranking members.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over antitrust law
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on February 7, 2019 and ordered the bill reported by voice vote.

for.name: 33 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support — 11 of 231 House Democrats and 22 of 197 House Republicans.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it cleared committee; no floor action occurred for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: OPEC member states
against.role: Foreign oil cartel whose production limits and pricing the bill targets
against.what_they_did: Opposed NOPEC legislation and lobbied against it, with member governments warning of retaliation against US interests.

sides.party_line_note: The 33 cosponsors split 22 Republicans and 11 Democrats, and the bill's original cosponsors included both the Democratic chairman (Nadler) and senior Republicans on the Judiciary Committee; it cleared committee by voice vote with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: These states restrict production and coordinate prices, which raises what consumers pay for fuel. The bill would let the US government sue them for that behavior in US courts, ending their legal shield.

Breaking up a cartel that restricts global supply would likely push world prices down, cutting revenue for US producers. US firms operating abroad could also face retaliation from oil-producing governments.
These companies buy crude as their main input; a more competitive, less cartel-controlled oil market would mean cheaper feedstock and better margins.
